KM_T_01.name: Immediately effective kamma
KM_T_01.description: Kamma that produces its result in the same life; if it cannot mature, it becomes defunct.
KM_T_01.doctrinalNote: Kamma that produces its result in the same life; if it cannot mature, it becomes defunct.

KM_T_02.name: Subsequently effective kamma
KM_T_02.description: Kamma that produces its result in the immediately following life.
KM_T_02.doctrinalNote: Kamma that produces its result in the immediately following life.

KM_T_03.name: Indefinitely effective kamma
KM_T_03.description: Kamma capable of producing results from the third life onward until final liberation.
KM_T_03.doctrinalNote: Kamma capable of producing results from the third life onward until final liberation.

KM_T_04.name: Defunct kamma
KM_T_04.description: Kamma whose opportunity to produce a result has passed.
KM_T_04.doctrinalNote: Kamma whose opportunity to produce a result has passed.

KM_P_01.name: Reproductive kamma
KM_P_01.description: Kamma that generates rebirth and the resultant aggregates of a new life.
KM_P_01.doctrinalNote: Kamma that generates rebirth and the resultant aggregates of a new life.

KM_P_02.name: Supportive kamma
KM_P_02.description: Kamma that supports and sustains the result of another kamma.
KM_P_02.doctrinalNote: Kamma that supports and sustains the result of another kamma.

KM_P_03.name: Obstructive kamma
KM_P_03.description: Kamma that obstructs or weakens the result of another kamma.
KM_P_03.doctrinalNote: Kamma that obstructs or weakens the result of another kamma.

KM_P_04.name: Destructive kamma
KM_P_04.description: Kamma that cuts off the result of another kamma and replaces it with its own result.
KM_P_04.doctrinalNote: Kamma that cuts off the result of another kamma and replaces it with its own result.

KM_U_01.name: Weighty kamma
KM_U_01.description: A very powerful wholesome or unwholesome kamma that takes priority in producing rebirth.
KM_U_01.doctrinalNote: A very powerful wholesome or unwholesome kamma that takes priority in producing rebirth.

KM_U_02.name: Death-proximate kamma
KM_U_02.description: Kamma remembered or performed close to death, influencing the next rebirth.
KM_U_02.doctrinalNote: Kamma remembered or performed close to death, influencing the next rebirth.

KM_U_03.name: Habitual kamma
KM_U_03.description: Kamma repeatedly performed until it becomes a strong habit.
KM_U_03.doctrinalNote: Kamma repeatedly performed until it becomes a strong habit.

KM_U_04.name: Cumulative kamma
KM_U_04.description: Accumulated kamma that produces a result when no stronger kamma takes priority.
KM_U_04.doctrinalNote: Accumulated kamma that produces a result when no stronger kamma takes priority.

KM_R_01.name: Unwholesome kamma
KM_R_01.description: Unwholesome kamma producing suffering - 12 unwholesome cittas produce 7 unwholesome rootless resultants and rebirth in 4 woeful planes.
KM_R_01.doctrinalNote: Akusala-kamma is the cause of dukkha, belonging to sense-sphere, resulting in woeful planes.

KM_R_02.name: Sense-sphere wholesome kamma
KM_R_02.description: Wholesome sense-sphere kamma producing happy sense-sphere results - 8 great wholesome cittas produce 8 great resultants and 7 wholesome rootless, rebirth as human or 6 deva planes.
KM_R_02.doctrinalNote: Kusala Duggati: wholesome resulting in happy sense-sphere, foundation for all merit.

KM_R_03.name: Form-sphere wholesome kamma
KM_R_03.description: Wholesome form-sphere kamma (5 form jhanas) producing form-sphere results - rebirth in 16 Brahma form planes, result is 5 form-sphere resultant cittas.
KM_R_03.doctrinalNote: Rupavacara-kamma belongs to exalted, beyond sense-sphere, giving result corresponding to jhana attained.

KM_R_04.name: Supramundane kamma (Path kamma)
KM_R_04.description: Supramundane kamma is the 4 Path cittas (Magga) - eradicating defilements and giving supramundane results as 4 Fruition cittas (Phala) and Nibbana, ending samsara.
KM_R_04.doctrinalNote: Lokuttara-kamma does not give rebirth in three planes but gives Nibbana - ultimate goal of VDP.

PD_01.name: Ignorance
PD_01.description: Ignorance is not knowing the Four Noble Truths, the three characteristics, kamma and its results, and dependent origination. It is the first root of the round of rebirth: without ignorance formations do not arise and the chain of dependent arising cannot form.
PD_01.characteristic: Not understanding — blindness to the true nature of things (the Four Truths, the three characteristics).
PD_01.function: To obscure clear seeing, and to serve as condition for the arising of formations.
PD_01.manifestation: As bewilderment and darkness — it keeps generating kamma (formations) without one realising it.
PD_01.proximateCause: Unwise attention (ayoniso-manasikāra); not meeting the wise and not hearing the True Dhamma.
PD_01.doctrinalNote: Avijjā has no discernible beginning (anamatagga). The ending of ignorance is the attainment of the four path consciousnesses.
examples: Not knowing this body is impermanent, one clings to it as a self and creates kamma to protect that self.

PD_02.name: Volitional formations
PD_02.description: Formations are kamma-forming activities — volition (cetanā) through the three doors of body, speech, and mind. They are of three kinds: meritorious formations (wholesome), demeritorious formations (unwholesome), and imperturbable formations (meditative attainments).
PD_02.characteristic: Acting and arranging — deliberate formation through body, speech, and mind.
PD_02.function: To generate kamma — accumulating kammic force that will yield rebirth in a future life.
PD_02.manifestation: As accumulated kamma that will draw consciousness into rebirth.
PD_02.proximateCause: Ignorance as condition (without ignorance, formations become supramundane and create no new kamma).
PD_02.doctrinalNote: Saṅkhārā in dependent origination means the volition (cetanā) mental factor that forms kamma.
examples: Giving with a wholesome mind is a meritorious formation; its consciousness rebirth-links into a good destination.
Attaining jhāna is an imperturbable formation; its consciousness rebirth-links as a Brahmā.

PD_03.name: Consciousness
PD_03.description: Consciousness here means chiefly the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-citta) — the first mind of this life, continuing from the previous life and carrying kamma's seed.
PD_03.characteristic: Knowing an object — the rebirth consciousness resting on the new mind-and-matter.
PD_03.function: To rebirth — to open a new life.
PD_03.manifestation: A new existence takes shape — mind-and-matter appear.
PD_03.proximateCause: Kamma (formations) as condition; mind-and-matter must be there to rest on.
PD_03.doctrinalNote: Consciousness and mind-and-matter lean on each other — like two sheaves of reeds propping one another up.
examples: At the moment of conception the rebirth-linking consciousness appears, mind-and-matter develop, and a new life begins.

PD_04.name: Mind and matter
PD_04.description: Mind-and-matter is the whole psycho-physical person: materiality (the body — the four great essentials and derived materiality) and mentality (consciousness together with its mental factors).
PD_04.characteristic: Existing — mind and body present and developing.
PD_04.function: To serve as the ground on which consciousness operates, and the condition for the six sense bases to develop.
PD_04.manifestation: The six sense bases become fully formed.
PD_04.proximateCause: Consciousness as condition; the four sources producing materiality.
examples: In the womb: rebirth consciousness appears and mind-and-matter gradually develop from embryo to full term.

PD_05.name: Six sense bases
PD_05.description: The six sense bases are the six places where objects are received: the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind bases — six doors through which the mind receives the six objects.
PD_05.characteristic: Readiness to receive — six doors through which objects enter.
PD_05.function: To serve as doors (dvāra) through which the mind meets outer objects.
PD_05.manifestation: Contact (phassa) is established — the mind can touch its object.
examples: A newborn child: with the six bases complete, contact with the outside world begins.

PD_06.name: Contact
PD_06.description: Contact is the meeting of three factors: sense base + object + consciousness. It is the condition for feeling to arise.
PD_06.characteristic: Touching — the encounter of base, object, and consciousness.
PD_06.function: To gather base, object, and consciousness together — conditioning the arising of feeling.
PD_06.manifestation: Mind, mental factors, base, and object come together.
PD_06.proximateCause: All three must be present: base + object + consciousness.
PD_06.doctrinalNote: Phassa in dependent origination is the contact mental factor (CS_PHASSA).
examples: The eye sees a lovely object: eye-base + visible object + eye-consciousness give eye-contact, and glad feeling follows.

PD_07.name: Feeling
PD_07.description: Feeling is the experience that follows contact — glad, sad, pleasant, painful, or neutral. This is the most important point of meditation practice: stop at feeling, and do not let feeling lead on to craving.
PD_07.characteristic: Experiencing — tasting the object as pleasant, painful, or neutral after contact.
PD_07.function: To enjoy the object — conditioning craving to arise when unwise attention prevails.
PD_07.manifestation: As pleasant, painful, or neutral experience forming in the mind.
PD_07.doctrinalNote: This is the crux of the four foundations of mindfulness: halt at feeling, and do not let it ripen into craving.
examples: Hearing praise (contact) brings glad feeling; without mindfulness, craving for more follows.

PD_08.name: Craving
PD_08.description: Craving is thirst, the intense wanting. It is of three kinds: craving for sense pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. Craving is the Truth of the Origin — the root of suffering.
PD_08.characteristic: Thirsting — the clinging wanting produced by feeling.
PD_08.function: To grasp at its object — conditioning the arising of clinging.
PD_08.manifestation: As clinging taking hold; the round of rebirth continues.
PD_08.proximateCause: Feeling (especially glad and pleasant feeling) as condition.
PD_08.doctrinalNote: Craving is the Origin of suffering among the Four Noble Truths. The ending of craving is the ending of suffering — Nibbāna.
examples: Seeing delicious food, craving arises: wanting to eat more.
Meeting pain, craving for non-existence arises: wanting not to be.

PD_09.name: Clinging
PD_09.description: Clinging is grasping tighter than craving. It is of four kinds: clinging to sense pleasures, to views, to rules and observances, and to a doctrine of self.
PD_09.characteristic: Holding tight — a grip that does not let go.
PD_09.function: To grasp the object firmly — conditioning the arising of becoming.
PD_09.manifestation: As becoming taking shape — rebirth-producing kamma accumulates.
PD_09.proximateCause: Craving as condition — clinging is craving intensified and consolidated.
examples: Not only wanting money (craving) but being unable to let money go (clinging).

PD_10.name: Becoming
PD_10.description: Becoming has two parts: kamma-becoming (kamma accumulated that will produce rebirth) and rebirth-becoming (the plane of existence into which rebirth will occur). There are three realms of becoming: sense-sphere, form-sphere, and formless-sphere becoming.
PD_10.characteristic: Existing — accumulated kammic force ready to produce rebirth.
PD_10.function: To condition birth taking place in a future life.
PD_10.manifestation: As rebirth occurring in a plane that matches the kamma.
PD_10.proximateCause: Clinging as condition — clinging is the fuel for becoming.
examples: One who gives generously all their life builds wholesome sense-sphere becoming and is reborn wealthy in the next life.

PD_11.name: Birth
PD_11.description: Birth is rebirth — the rebirth-linking consciousness appearing in a new life, mind-and-matter forming, the aggregates arising. All suffering begins here.
PD_11.characteristic: Rebirth-linking — consciousness reborn into a new plane.
PD_11.function: To open a new life — dragging the whole mass of suffering along.
PD_11.doctrinalNote: The three-life circle joins here: birth (PD_11) corresponds to consciousness (PD_03) on the result side of the future life.
examples: The moment of conception is birth — all suffering follows from it.

PD_12.name: Ageing and death
PD_12.description: Ageing-and-death: ageing is growing old and decaying; death is falling. Together with them come sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair — all the suffering of a life. It is the final result that closes one life and, if there is no liberation, opens a new round.
PD_12.characteristic: Ageing and dying — the inevitable decay and perishing of all conditioned mind and body.
PD_12.function: To end a life — and to continue a new round of becoming if liberation has not been won.
PD_12.manifestation: A life closed; without liberation the round continues.
PD_12.proximateCause: Birth as condition — where there is birth, ageing-and-death necessarily follow.
PD_12.doctrinalNote: Liberation means ending ignorance (PD_01) and craving (PD_08) — the realisation of Nibbāna.
examples: Every being that has been born must age and die.
When ignorance and craving are destroyed, ageing-and-death no longer follow.

VT_NGU_MON_RATLON.name: Atimahanta-ārammaṇa Pañcadvāra-vīthi
VT_NGU_MON_RATLON.description: The most complete process — it arises when a five-sense object strikes very strongly. All 17 mind-moments occur: 2 vibrating and 1 arresting bhavaṅga, 5 rootless cittas, 7 impulsions, and 2 registrations.
VT_NGU_MON_RATLON.arisingCondition: A five-sense object (visible form, sound, odour, taste, tangibility) strikes its corresponding sense base very strongly.
VT_NGU_MON_RATLON.significance: The most complete process — the 7 impulsions create kamma in full, and registration enjoys the residual object.
VT_NGU_MON_RATLON.doctrinalNote: Atimahanta = an object great enough to allow Javana × 7 plus Tadārammaṇa × 2.

1.name: Past bhavaṅga
1.description: The life-continuum flowing along normally before the object strikes.
1.doctrinalNote: The same class of citta as this person's rebirth-linking and dying consciousness.

2.name: Vibrating bhavaṅga
2.description: The object strikes the sense base and the life-continuum vibrates for the first time.

3.name: Arrest bhavaṅga
3.description: The bhavaṅga stream is fully cut off — the cognitive process begins.
3.doctrinalNote: After this moment the five-door adverting consciousness arises.

4.name: Five-door adverting
4.description: Opens the five-sense door and turns toward the object, determining which door the object has struck.
4.doctrinalNote: CI_028 — equanimity feeling, 11 mental factors. Creates no kamma.

5.name: Five-fold sense consciousness
5.description: Knows the object through the corresponding sense door. Only the seven universal mental factors accompany it.
5.doctrinalNote: Unwholesome-resultant (CI_013–017) or wholesome-resultant (CI_020–024), according to rebirth kamma.

6.name: Receiving
6.description: Receives the object from the sense consciousness and passes it into the inner stream of consciousness.
6.doctrinalNote: CI_018 = unwholesome-resultant with equanimity; CI_025 = wholesome-resultant with equanimity. 10 mental factors.

7.name: Investigating
7.description: Examines the object — determining whether it is good or bad, pleasing or not.
7.doctrinalNote: CI_027 (with joy) appears only when the object is very beautiful.

8.name: Determining
8.description: Makes the final determination of the object as good or bad — opening the way for the 7 impulsions.
8.doctrinalNote: CI_029 (mind-door adverting) plays the role of determining. 11 mental factors. It decides the kind of javana that follows.

9.name: Impulsion (Javana)
9.description: Seven consecutive impulsion moments — creating wholesome or unwholesome kamma. Moment 1 bears fruit in this very life; moment 7 in the next life; moments 2–6 in later lives.
9.doctrinalNote: 7 moments of one and the same class of citta. The only part of the process that creates kamma.

10.name: Registration (Tadārammaṇa)
10.description: Two registration moments enjoying the residual object after the impulsions. They occur only in a very-great-object process and create no new kamma.
10.doctrinalNote: Tadā = 'then'; ārammaṇa = object. They arise only when the object is great enough.

11.name: Post-process bhavaṅga
11.description: After the process ends, the life-continuum resumes its normal flow.

VT_NGU_MON_LON.name: Mahanta-ārammaṇa Pañcadvāra-vīthi
VT_NGU_MON_LON.description: A five-door process with the full 7 impulsions but NO registration — the object is not strong enough for tadārammaṇa to arise.
VT_NGU_MON_LON.arisingCondition: A five-sense object strong enough for 7 impulsions, but not strong enough to produce registration.
VT_NGU_MON_LON.significance: The most ordinary process — kamma is created in full through the 7 impulsions.
VT_NGU_MON_LON.doctrinalNote: It differs from the very-great-object process only in lacking the 2 registration moments.

1.name: Vibrating bhavaṅga
1.description: The life-continuum vibrates as the object strikes the sense base.

2.name: Arrest bhavaṅga
2.description: The bhavaṅga stream is cut off — the process begins.

3.name: Five-door adverting
3.description: Turns the mind toward the object through the five-sense door.

4.name: Five-fold sense consciousness
4.description: Knows the object through the corresponding sense.

7.name: Determining
7.description: Determines the object, opening the way for the impulsions.

8.name: Impulsion (Javana)
8.description: Seven impulsion moments create kamma. Afterwards there is NO registration.
8.doctrinalNote: After the 7 impulsions the mind drops straight back into the life-continuum.

9.name: Post-process bhavaṅga
9.description: The life-continuum resumes after the process.

VT_Y_MON.name: Manodvāra-vīthi
VT_Y_MON.description: The mind-door process arises when the mind contacts a mind object through the mind door — thinking, remembering, imagining. Immediately after the mind-door adverting consciousness come the 7 impulsions.
VT_Y_MON.arisingCondition: A mind object (dhammārammaṇa) appears at the mind door — a thought, a memory, an imagination.
VT_Y_MON.significance: It explains all inner mental activity. It creates mind-kamma, and is the wellspring of verbal and bodily kamma.
VT_Y_MON.doctrinalNote: The mind-door process begins with the mind-door adverting consciousness (CI_029), without passing through five-door adverting.

1.name: Vibrating bhavaṅga
1.description: The life-continuum vibrates as the mind object strikes.

2.name: Arrest bhavaṅga
2.description: The life-continuum is arrested — the mind-door process begins.

3.name: Mind-door adverting
3.description: Opens the mind door and directs the mind to the mind object, at the same time determining it (serving as determining within this process).
3.doctrinalNote: CI_029 serves both as mind-door adverting and as determining. 11 mental factors.

4.name: Impulsion (Javana)
4.description: Seven impulsion moments — creating mind-kamma. All deliberate thought, speech, and action arise here.
4.doctrinalNote: Creates mind-kamma directly. Verbal and bodily kamma also begin at the mind door.

5.name: Registration (optional)
5.description: Registration in the mind-door process — depending on the strength of the mind object.

VT_VITHIMUTTA.name: Vīthimutta-citta
VT_VITHIMUTTA.description: Vīthimutta are consciousnesses operating outside the cognitive process — through no door at all. They have three functions: rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and death (cuti). All three use the same type of consciousness.
VT_VITHIMUTTA.arisingCondition: Rebirth-linking: when the previous life ends. Life-continuum: between processes. Death: when the material life faculty perishes.
VT_VITHIMUTTA.significance: It explains the mechanism of rebirth and the linkage between lives.
VT_VITHIMUTTA.doctrinalNote: Process-free consciousness creates no new kamma — it is kammically indeterminate resultant mind.

1.name: Rebirth-linking consciousness
1.description: The first consciousness of the new life — continuing directly from the previous life's dying consciousness, carrying kamma's seed.
1.doctrinalNote: CI_019/CI_026 = a two-rooted person; CI_027 = a specially favoured person; CI_063–CI_070 = a three-rooted person or a deva.

2.name: Life-continuum consciousness
2.description: The stream of consciousness that sustains the life between processes. It arises and passes innumerable times, and is the foundation of all mental activity.
2.doctrinalNote: Bhavaṅga = the life-maintaining part of the stream. It runs in deep sleep and between processes.

3.name: Death consciousness
3.description: The final mind-moment — the material life faculty perishes, the death consciousness falls, and the life ends. Immediately afterwards the next life's rebirth-linking consciousness arises.
3.doctrinalNote: Cuti = to move on, to depart. The object of the death consciousness is the death-proximate (āsanna) object.

M1_BASICS.title: Seven universal cetasikas
M1_BASICS.description: The seven mental factors present in every citta; the foundation for all later modules.

lessonSections.title: The Aññasamāna group and the universal factors
body: This paragraph explains the relevant Dhamma as taught in the source.
The Aññasamāna group is divided into two: the universal factors (Sabbacittasādhāraṇa), seven in number, and the occasional factors (Pakiṇṇaka), six in number.
The seven universal mental factors are: Contact (Phassa), Feeling (Vedanā), Perception (Saññā), Volition (Cetanā), One-pointedness (Ekaggatā), Life faculty (Jīvitindriya) and Attention (Manasikāra).
They are called 'universal' because all seven arise together with every citta without exception.

sourceRefs.note: TÂM SỞ TỢ THA – AÑÑASAMĀNA; liệt kê Biến hành 7 và Biệt cảnh 6

lessonSections.title: Contact (Phassa) and Feeling (Vedanā)
body: Phassa comes from the root 'phas' — to touch, to contact, to impinge. Whenever consciousness meets its object, the mental factor of contact is present.

In the five-aggregate existence, when a sense base (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body) meets its corresponding object (visible form, sound, odour, taste, tangible object) consciousness arises — at that moment contact is present. Each base contacts only its own object.
In the four-mental-aggregate existence (the immaterial sphere, where no materiality exists), contact requires only object and consciousness impinging on each other.
Vedanā comes from the root 'vid' — to feel, to experience. When an object impinges on the mental stream, feeling receives and experiences that object.
An important relationship: contact is nutriment for feeling — because of contact, feeling arises; hence it is called 'contact as nutriment' (phassa-āhāra).

lessonSections.title: Perception (Saññā) and Volition (Cetanā)
body: Saññā = saṃ + ñā: to know what has been known before, to remember and recognise something through its mark.
Perception is classified by kind into three: unwholesome, wholesome and indeterminate; and by object into six (form-perception, sound-perception, etc.).
Cetanā, citta and cetasika all derive from the root 'cit' — to think, to consider. Volition is the most important mental factor.
The special task of volition is twofold: it performs its own function and it organises the activity of the other co-arisen mental factors — and it is volition that creates kamma.

lessonSections.title: One-pointedness, Life faculty and Attention
body: Ekaggatā: eka (one) + agga (peak) — one-pointedness, concentration. It gathers citta and its co-arisen mental factors onto a single object, holding the mind steady without wavering.
Jīvitindriya: jīvita (life, maintaining) + indriya (faculty, controlling). The life faculty governs the existence of co-arisen phenomena.

There are two kinds: mental life faculty maintains mentality for three sub-moments (arising, presence, dissolution); material life faculty maintains materiality for 51 sub-moments (17 mind-moments × 3).
Manasikāra: manasī (mind) + kāra (making) — making in the mind, i.e., attention. It gathers the object to make it the citta's object.

The fourfold definition of attention: characteristic — directing associated phenomena to the object; function — yoking co-arisen mind and mental factors to the object; manifestation — facing the object; proximate cause — the object.

reviewCards.front: What does "Aññasamāna" mean?
reviewCards.back: Añña means "other"; Samāna means "common" -> "common to the other" (ethically variable). They become wholesome or unwholesome depending on the citta they accompany.

reviewCards.front: List the seven Universal mental factors (Sabbacittasādhāraṇa).
reviewCards.back: Contact (Phassa), Feeling (Vedanā), Perception (Saññā), Volition (Cetanā), One-pointedness (Ekaggatā), Life Faculty (Jīvitindriya), and Attention (Manasikāra).

reviewCards.front: Why are they called "Universal" (Sabbacittasādhāraṇa)?
reviewCards.back: Because all seven mental factors arise in every single consciousness without exception.

reviewCards.front: How many Occasional mental factors (Pakiṇṇaka) are there?
reviewCards.back: 6: Applied Thought (Vitakka), Sustained Thought (Vicāra), Decision (Adhimokkha), Energy (Vīriya), Joy (Pīti), and Desire (Chanda).

reviewCards.front: From what root does "Phassa" derive and what does it mean?
reviewCards.back: Root "phas": to touch, make contact, or encounter an objective datum.

reviewCards.front: What is the relationship between Contact (Phassa) and Feeling (Vedanā)?
reviewCards.back: Contact serves as nutriment for feeling (contact-nutriment) — with contact as condition, feeling arises.

reviewCards.front: How is "Saññā" analyzed etymologically?
reviewCards.back: Saññā = saṃ + ñā: recognizing what was previously known, noting marks and signs for subsequent recall.

reviewCards.front: From what root do Cetanā, Citta, and Cetasika originate?
reviewCards.back: From the root "CIT": to cognize, think, or reflect.

reviewCards.front: Why is Volition (Cetanā) considered the most vital mental factor in action?
reviewCards.back: Because volition organizes and coordinates associated mental factors, and volition itself is that which constitutes kamma.

reviewCards.front: How is "Ekaggatā" analyzed etymologically?
reviewCards.back: Eka (one) + agga (point/apex) -> one-pointedness, unification of mind, mental stillness.

reviewCards.front: How long does Mental Life Faculty preserve mental states?
reviewCards.back: For 3 sub-moments: arising (uppāda), presence (ṭhiti), and dissolution (bhaṅga).

reviewCards.front: How long does Physical Life Faculty preserve material phenomena?
reviewCards.back: For 51 sub-moments = 17 thought-moments × 3 sub-moments.

reviewCards.front: How is "Manasikāra" analyzed etymologically?
reviewCards.back: Manasi (in the mind) + kāra (making/doing) -> making in the mind, attention directing mind to the object.

reviewCards.front: What is the function of Attention (Manasikāra)?
reviewCards.back: Directing and harnessing consciousness and associated mental factors onto the object.

quizSeeds.question: How many Universal mental factors (Sabbacittasādhāraṇa) are there?
quizSeeds.explanation: There are 7 Universal mental factors present in every citta: phassa, vedanā, saññā, cetanā, ekaggatā, jīvitindriya, and manasikāra.

quizSeeds.question: Which mental factor does NOT belong to the Universals?
quizSeeds.explanation: Applied Thought (Vitakka) is an Occasional (Pakiṇṇaka) mental factor, not a Universal.

quizSeeds.question: What does "Aññasamāna" mean?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: Common to the other — becoming wholesome or unwholesome depending on associated citta
quizSeeds.explanation: Aññasamāna mental factors take on the moral quality of whatever consciousness they arise with.

quizSeeds.question: What is Contact (Phassa)?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: The touching or encounter between consciousness and the object
distractors: The affective experience of the object
Remembering the mark of the object
quizSeeds.explanation: Contact has the characteristic of touching (phusanā) the object.

quizSeeds.question: What does "contact-nutriment" (phassāhāra) mean?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: Contact serves as condition/nutriment that brings about feeling
distractors: Contact is the food of perception
quizSeeds.explanation: In the discourses, contact is the nutriment for feeling (phassapaccayā vedanā).

quizSeeds.question: What is the primary function of Perception (Saññā)?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: To recognize and note through previously known marks and signs
distractors: To sustain the life of mental states
quizSeeds.explanation: Saññā marks the object so that it can be recognized again later.

quizSeeds.question: Which mental factor constitutes the essence of kamma?
quizSeeds.explanation: The Buddha taught: "Cetanāhaṃ, bhikkhave, kammaṃ vadāmi" — It is volition that I call kamma.

quizSeeds.question: From which words is "Ekaggatā" derived?
quizSeeds.explanation: Ekaggatā literally means one-pointedness of mind.

quizSeeds.question: For how many sub-moments does Physical Life Faculty preserve matter?
quizSeeds.explanation: A material phenomenon lasts for 17 thought-moments, and each thought-moment consists of 3 sub-moments, giving 51 sub-moments.

quizSeeds.question: For how many sub-moments does Mental Life Faculty preserve mental states?
quizSeeds.explanation: Mental states endure for only 1 thought-moment, which has 3 sub-moments.

quizSeeds.question: What is the function (kicca) of Attention (Manasikāra)?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: To steer and direct associated mental states onto the object
distractors: To experience the flavour of the object
To remember marks of the object
To govern the existence of states
quizSeeds.explanation: Manasikāra acts like a helmsman directing consciousness to its objective field.

quizSeeds.question: In the Formless Realm (four mental aggregates), how does Contact arise?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: Simply through the contact between consciousness and the mental object
distractors: Requiring physical nerve matter as support
quizSeeds.explanation: In the formless realm, there is no physical matter, so contact arises purely between mind and mental object.

reviewCards.front: What does Occasional (Pakiṇṇaka) mean?
reviewCards.back: Mental factors that arise only in CERTAIN cittas (scattered), unlike Universals which arise in all cittas.

reviewCards.front: What are the six Occasional mental factors?
reviewCards.back: Applied Thought (Vitakka), Sustained Thought (Vicāra), Decision (Adhimokkha), Energy (Vīriya), Joy (Pīti), and Desire (Chanda).

reviewCards.front: What does "Vitakka" mean?
reviewCards.back: "Vi" (distinctive) + root "takk" (to think/reflect) -> thinking or reflecting distinctly; directing the mind onto the object.

reviewCards.front: What is the chief characteristic of Applied Thought (Vitakka)?
reviewCards.back: Lifting the associated mental factors onto the object — mounting or striking the mind onto the object.

reviewCards.front: What does "Vicāra" mean?
reviewCards.back: Examining the object, wandering around the object, keeping the mind continuously anchored and investigating closely.

reviewCards.front: What analogies distinguish Vitakka from Vicāra?
reviewCards.back: Vitakka: bee flying straight to a lotus, bird flapping wings to take off, striking a gong. Vicāra: bee circling around the lotus, bird soaring smoothly in the sky, humming reverberation of the gong.

reviewCards.front: In which group of cittas do Vitakka and Vicāra NOT arise?
reviewCards.back: The Twofold Fivefold Sense Consciousness (dvi-pañcaviññāṇa, 10 cittas): eye, ear, nose, tongue, body consciousness — because they perform purely receptive functions without reflection.

reviewCards.front: What does "Adhimokkha" mean?
reviewCards.back: Adhi + muc (to release): releasing the mind from indecision toward the object — conviction, decision, resolute determination.

reviewCards.front: In how many cittas is Decision (Adhimokkha) present?
reviewCards.back: 110 cittas (121 total − 10 twofold sense consciousness − 1 delusion accompanied by doubt).

reviewCards.front: What are the four characteristics of Energy (Vīriya)?
reviewCards.back: Characteristic: endurance and effort. Function: supporting associated states from collapsing. Manifestation: non-collapse. Proximate cause: sense of urgency (saṃvega) or grounds for stirring effort.

reviewCards.front: What are the Four Right Efforts (Sammappadhāna)?
reviewCards.back: Effort to prevent unarisen evil, effort to abandon arisen evil, effort to arouse unarisen wholesome states, effort to maintain arisen wholesome states.

reviewCards.front: What are the three kinds of Desire (Chanda)?
reviewCards.back: Chanda-rāga (sensual lust), Kusala-chanda / Dhamma-chanda (righteous aspiration for wholesome deeds), and Kiriya-chanda (functional desire of Arahants to act).

quizSeeds.question: How many Occasional mental factors (Pakiṇṇaka) are there?
quizSeeds.explanation: There are 6 Occasionals: vitakka, vicāra, adhimokkha, vīriya, pīti, and chanda.

quizSeeds.question: Which mental factor does NOT belong to the Occasionals?
quizSeeds.explanation: Attention (Manasikāra) is a Universal mental factor, not an Occasional.

quizSeeds.question: What is the primary meaning of "Vitakka"?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: Directing and applying the mind distinctly onto the object
distractors: Circling and examining around the object
quizSeeds.explanation: Vitakka has the characteristic of directing the mind onto the object (ārammaṇe cittassa abhiniropana).

quizSeeds.question: Which simile illustrates Sustained Thought (Vicāra)?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: A bee circling and hovering around the lotus flower
distractors: A bee flying directly to strike the lotus
A bird flapping wings to take flight
Striking a gong with a mallet
quizSeeds.explanation: Vicāra is likened to the bee buzzing and examining around the blossom after Vitakka has brought it there.

quizSeeds.question: In which group of cittas are Vitakka and Vicāra absent?
quizSeeds.explanation: The 10 sense consciousnesses are passive and primitive, lacking applied and sustained thought.

quizSeeds.question: What does "Adhimokkha" literally mean?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: Releasing the mind from doubt into resolute decision
distractors: Lifting mental states onto the object
quizSeeds.explanation: Adhimokkha literally means unshakeable decision or conviction, freeing the mind from hesitation.

quizSeeds.question: In how many cittas is Decision (Adhimokkha) present?
quizSeeds.explanation: Adhimokkha is found in 110 cittas, excluded only from the 10 sense consciousnesses and 1 delusion citta with doubt.

quizSeeds.question: What are the Four Right Efforts?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: Preventing unarisen evil, abandoning arisen evil, arousing unarisen good, maintaining arisen good
distractors: Preventing evil, abandoning good, developing wisdom, guarding mindfulness
Stirring energy, guarding sense doors, suppressing anger, resting calmly
quizSeeds.explanation: The Four Right Efforts (Sammappadhāna) cover avoiding and overcoming unwholesome states, and developing and maintaining wholesome states.

quizSeeds.question: How many degrees of Joy (Pīti) are classified in meditation texts?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: 5 — from minor joy to all-pervading joy
quizSeeds.explanation: The five kinds of pīti are: khuddikā (minor), khaṇikā (momentary), okkantikā (showering), ubbegā (uplifting), and pharaṇā (all-pervading).

quizSeeds.question: What is the nature of Joy in Arahants?
quizSeeds.explanation: In an Arahant, joy is purely functional (kiriya) without karmic potency.

quizSeeds.question: What is the will to act in an Arahant termed?
quizSeeds.explanation: The desire to act in an Arahant is purely functional desire (kiriya-chanda), free from defilements.

quizSeeds.question: In which cittas is Desire (Chanda) absent?
quizSeeds.explanation: Chanda does not arise in the 2 delusion-rooted cittas or the 18 rootless cittas (20 cittas in total).

M2_SI_PHAN.description: Delusion, shamelessness, fearlessness of wrongdoing, and restlessness accompany every unwholesome citta.

lessonSections.title: Unwholesome factors and the delusion group
body: The unwholesome mental factors comprise 14 cetasikas, divided into several groups.
Akusala (unwholesome) has five meanings: (1) diseased, bringing suffering; (2) unlovely, foul; (3) unskilful, clouded by greed-hatred-delusion; (4) faulty; (5) productive of painful results.

The delusion group (mocatuka) comprises four cetasikas: delusion (moha), shamelessness (ahirika), fearlessness of wrongdoing (anottappa) and restlessness (uddhacca). They are called 'unwholesome universals' because they accompany every unwholesome citta.

reviewCards.front: How many Unwholesome mental factors (Akusala cetasika) are there?
reviewCards.back: 14 unwholesome mental factors (Akusala cetasika).

reviewCards.front: What are the five meanings of "Akusala"?
reviewCards.back: Unhealthy; blameworthy; unskilful; faulty/erroneous; producing painful result.

reviewCards.front: Which mental factors make up the Delusion-tetrad (Moha-catukka)?
reviewCards.back: Delusion (Moha), Shamelessness (Ahirika), Fearlessness of wrongdoing (Anottappa), and Restlessness (Uddhacca).

reviewCards.front: Why is the Delusion-tetrad called "Unwholesome Universals" (Akusala-sādhāraṇa)?
reviewCards.back: Because all four arise in every single one of the 12 unwholesome cittas.

reviewCards.front: What is Shamelessness (Ahirika)?
reviewCards.back: Lack of moral shame; having no shame or embarrassment in committing unwholesome deeds.

reviewCards.front: What is Fearlessness of wrongdoing (Anottappa)?
reviewCards.back: Lack of moral dread; having no fear or shrink from the dreadful consequences of unwholesome actions.

reviewCards.front: Can Ahirika and Anottappa occur separately?
reviewCards.back: No. They always arise together — wherever there is absence of moral dread, there is also absence of moral shame.

reviewCards.front: How is "Uddhacca" analyzed etymologically?
reviewCards.back: U (up/above) + root dhu (to shake/waver) -> wavering above, turmoil, mental agitation or restlessness.

reviewCards.front: What analogies illustrate Restlessness (Uddhacca)?
reviewCards.back: Horse hooves immediately lifting upon touching ground; fish flopping frantically out of water; gathering clouds blown away by wind; dust scattered in wind.

reviewCards.front: Restlessness is a hindrance (nīvaraṇa) opposing which jhāna factor?
reviewCards.back: Restlessness is a hindrance opposing the jhāna factor of Bliss/Happiness (Sukha).

quizSeeds.question: How many mental factors comprise the Delusion-tetrad (Moha-catukka)?
quizSeeds.explanation: The Delusion-tetrad comprises Moha, Ahirika, Anottappa, and Uddhacca.

quizSeeds.question: Why is the Delusion-tetrad called "Unwholesome Universals"?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: Because they arise in all 12 unwholesome consciousnesses
distractors: Because they arise in every single consciousness
Because they exist only in 2 delusion cittas
Because they arise in both wholesome and unwholesome cittas
quizSeeds.explanation: Every unwholesome state is invariably accompanied by delusion, shamelessness, fearlessness of wrongdoing, and restlessness.

quizSeeds.question: How many Unwholesome mental factors (Akusala cetasikas) are there in total?
quizSeeds.explanation: There are 14 unwholesome cetasikas: 4 delusion group, 3 greed group, 4 hatred group, 2 sloth and torpor, and 1 doubt.

quizSeeds.question: What does Ahirika mean?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: Moral shamelessness — lack of shame in wrongdoing
distractors: Moral dreadlessness — lack of fear of consequences
quizSeeds.explanation: Ahirika has the characteristic of absence of shame (alajjā) regarding bodily or mental evil.

quizSeeds.question: What is the relationship between Ahirika and Anottappa?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: They always arise together in all unwholesome cittas
distractors: They arise together only in hatred cittas
They arise together only in delusion cittas
quizSeeds.explanation: Shamelessness and fearlessness of wrongdoing invariably co-arise in every unwholesome state.

quizSeeds.question: What is the state of Uddhacca (Restlessness)?
quizSeeds.explanation: Uddhacca has the characteristic of mental disquietude or flurry, like water stirred by wind.

quizSeeds.question: In how many unwholesome cittas is Restlessness (Uddhacca) present?
quizSeeds.explanation: As part of the Delusion-tetrad, Uddhacca is present in all 12 unwholesome cittas.

quizSeeds.question: How many meanings of "Akusala" are enumerated in the Abhidhamma teaching?
quizSeeds.explanation: Akusala signifies: unhealthy, blameworthy, unskilful, faulty, and producing painful vipāka.

quizSeeds.question: Which jhāna factor is directly opposed by Restlessness (Uddhacca)?
quizSeeds.explanation: Restlessness agitates the mind, directly opposing the peace and bliss (sukha) of deep meditation.

quizSeeds.question: What role does the Delusion-tetrad play regarding other unwholesome mental factors?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: They serve as the universal foundation leading all unwholesome states
quizSeeds.explanation: Moha, ahirika, anottappa, and uddhacca form the universal matrix for every unwholesome mind state.

reviewCards.front: How many Unwholesome cittas are there and how are they classified?
reviewCards.back: 12 cittas: 8 Greed-rooted (Lobhamūla), 2 Hatred-rooted (Dosamūla), and 2 Delusion-rooted (Mohamūla).

reviewCards.front: How many Sense-sphere cittas are there and what groups do they form?
reviewCards.back: 54 cittas: 12 Unwholesome + 18 Rootless + 24 Sense-sphere Beautiful.

reviewCards.front: What are the four aspects (lakkhaṇādicatukka) of Consciousness (Citta)?
reviewCards.back: Characteristic: cognizing the object. Function: leading associated mental factors. Manifestation: continuous unbroken series. Proximate cause: mentality-materiality and object.

reviewCards.front: What are the four causes for the arising of Consciousness?
reviewCards.back: Past kamma; object-condition; associated mental factors; physical base.

reviewCards.front: By what three pairs of opposites are the 8 Greed-rooted cittas classified?
reviewCards.back: Joy/equanimity; Associated/dissociated from wrong view; Unprompted/prompted -> 2×2×2 = 8.

reviewCards.front: From which root does "Lobha" come?
reviewCards.back: Root "lub": to cling, stick to, yearn, or crave.

reviewCards.front: In terms of kammic potency, which greed-rooted cittas are stronger?
reviewCards.back: Joy > equanimity; Unprompted > prompted; Associated with wrong view > dissociated from wrong view.

reviewCards.front: What do "Asaṅkhārika" and "Sasaṅkhārika" mean?
reviewCards.back: Asaṅkhārika: unprompted (spontaneous, without instigation). Sasaṅkhārika: prompted (induced with prompting or hesitation).

reviewCards.front: In what way do the two Hatred-rooted cittas differ?
reviewCards.back: Both are accompanied by displeasure and associated with aversion; they differ only in being unprompted (spontaneous) or prompted (induced).

reviewCards.front: What are four causes for the arising of Hatred-rooted consciousness?
reviewCards.back: Habitual wrathful temperament; lack of wise reflection; deficiency in spiritual learning; frequent encounter with disagreeable objects.

reviewCards.front: What are the names of the two Delusion-rooted cittas?
reviewCards.back: Delusion accompanied by equanimity and associated with doubt (vicikicchā), and Delusion accompanied by equanimity and associated with restlessness (uddhacca).

reviewCards.front: What does Skeptical Doubt (Vicikicchā) specifically doubt?
reviewCards.back: The Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, the Three Trainings, past lives, future lives, past-and-future, and Dependent Origination.

reviewCards.front: What are the two causes for the arising of Delusion-rooted consciousness?
reviewCards.back: Unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) and underlying latent taints (sensuality, existence, views, ignorance).

reviewCards.front: What feeling accompanies both Delusion-rooted cittas?
reviewCards.back: Both are accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā-sahagata).

reviewCards.front: Which mental factors make up the Greed-triad (Lobha-triad)?
reviewCards.back: 3: Greed (Lobha), Wrong View (Diṭṭhi), and Conceit (Māna).

reviewCards.front: In which cittas do Wrong View and Conceit arise?
reviewCards.back: Wrong View (Diṭṭhi): in the 4 greed cittas associated with wrong view. Conceit (Māna): in the 4 greed cittas dissociated from wrong view.

reviewCards.front: Which mental factors make up the Hatred-tetrad (Dosa-tetrad)?
reviewCards.back: 4: Hatred (Dosa), Envy (Issā), Avarice (Macchariya), and Remorse (Kukkucca) — arising only in the 2 hatred cittas.

reviewCards.front: What are the characteristics of Sloth and Torpor (Thīna-middha)?
reviewCards.back: Sloth (Thīna): unwieldiness and shrinking of mind, opposing energy. Torpor (Middha): sluggishness and drowsiness of mental factors. Both arise only in the 5 prompted unwholesome cittas.

reviewCards.front: In which citta does Doubt (Vicikicchā) arise?
reviewCards.back: Only in Delusion-rooted citta accompanied by equanimity and associated with doubt.

reviewCards.front: How are the 14 Unwholesome mental factors classified into groups?
reviewCards.back: 5 groups: Delusion-tetrad (4), Greed-triad (3), Hatred-tetrad (4), Sloth-torpor pair (2), and Doubt (1).

quizSeeds.question: How are the 12 Unwholesome cittas classified?
quizSeeds.explanation: The 12 unwholesome cittas comprise 8 lobhamūla, 2 dosamūla, and 2 mohamūla cittas.

quizSeeds.question: How many Sense-sphere cittas are there?
quizSeeds.explanation: The 54 sense-sphere cittas consist of 12 unwholesome, 18 rootless, and 24 sense-sphere beautiful cittas.

quizSeeds.question: By which three pairs of opposites are the 8 Greed cittas differentiated?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: Joy/equanimity — Associated/dissociated from wrong view — Unprompted/prompted
quizSeeds.explanation: The 8 greed-rooted cittas vary by feeling (somanassa/upekkhā), wrong view (diṭṭhigata-sampayutta/vippayutta), and instigation (asaṅkhārika/sasaṅkhārika).

quizSeeds.question: What does "Asaṅkhārika" mean?
quizSeeds.explanation: Asaṅkhārika means arising spontaneously of its own accord without prompting or deliberation.

quizSeeds.question: From which root does "Lobha" derive?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: Root "lub" — to cling or attach to
quizSeeds.explanation: Lobha comes from the root lub, meaning to desire, lust after, or adhere to an object.

quizSeeds.question: What feeling accompanies Hatred-rooted consciousness?
quizSeeds.explanation: Hatred-rooted consciousness is invariably accompanied by mental unpleasantness or displeasure (domanassa).

quizSeeds.question: How many Hatred-rooted cittas are there?
quizSeeds.explanation: There are 2 hatred-rooted cittas: unprompted and prompted, both accompanied by displeasure and associated with ill-will.

quizSeeds.question: What feeling accompanies both Delusion-rooted cittas?
distractors: One with joy and one with equanimity
quizSeeds.explanation: Both delusion-rooted cittas (with doubt and with restlessness) are accompanied by neutral feeling (upekkhā).

quizSeeds.question: Which delusion citta is associated with Vicikicchā?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: Delusion citta accompanied by equanimity and associated with doubt
distractors: Delusion citta accompanied by equanimity and associated with restlessness
quizSeeds.explanation: Skeptical doubt (vicikicchā) is associated exclusively with the first delusion-rooted citta.

quizSeeds.question: What are the two primary causes for the arising of Delusion-rooted consciousness?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: Unwise attention and underlying latent taints
quizSeeds.explanation: Delusion arises primarily through improper reflection (ayoniso manasikāra) supported by underlying dormant defilements (āsavas).

quizSeeds.question: Which greed-rooted citta produces stronger kammic result according to the Abhidhamma?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: Accompanied by joy is stronger than accompanied by equanimity
distractors: Accompanied by equanimity is stronger than accompanied by joy
Dissociated from wrong view is stronger than associated
quizSeeds.explanation: Joyful, unprompted cittas associated with wrong view produce heavier unwholesome kamma than their counterparts.

quizSeeds.question: What is the defining characteristic (lakkhaṇa) of Consciousness (Citta)?
quizSeeds.explanation: Citta has the fundamental characteristic of cognizing or being aware of the object (vijānanalakkhaṇaṃ).

quizSeeds.question: How many mental factors comprise the Greed-triad?
quizSeeds.explanation: The lobha-triad consists of Lobha, Diṭṭhi, and Māna.

quizSeeds.question: In which cittas does Wrong View (Diṭṭhi) arise?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: 4 Greed cittas associated with wrong view
distractors: 4 Greed cittas dissociated from wrong view
quizSeeds.explanation: Wrong view arises only in the four greed-rooted cittas that are diṭṭhigata-sampayutta.

quizSeeds.question: In which cittas does Conceit (Māna) arise?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: 4 Greed cittas dissociated from wrong view
distractors: 4 Greed cittas associated with wrong view
quizSeeds.explanation: Conceit can only arise in greed-rooted cittas that are dissociated from wrong view (diṭṭhigata-vippayutta).

quizSeeds.question: Which mental factors make up the Hatred-tetrad?
quizSeeds.explanation: The dosa-tetrad comprises Dosa, Issā, Macchariya, and Kukkucca.

quizSeeds.question: What is Envy (Issā)?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: Jealousy and resentment at the success and fortune of others
distractors: Concealing and guarding one's own prosperity
quizSeeds.explanation: Issā has the characteristic of envying others' prosperity and good fortune.

quizSeeds.question: What is Avarice (Macchariya)?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: Stinginess — concealing and refusing to share one's own prosperity
distractors: Jealousy at the achievement of others
quizSeeds.explanation: Macchariya has the characteristic of concealing one's own success and unwillingness to share.

quizSeeds.question: Which wholesome factor is directly opposed by Sloth (Thīna)?
quizSeeds.explanation: Sloth is mental sluggishness and shrinking, directly opposing the rousing quality of Energy (Vīriya).

quizSeeds.question: In which citta does Skeptical Doubt (Vicikicchā) arise?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: Delusion citta accompanied by equanimity and associated with doubt
quizSeeds.explanation: Vicikicchā arises uniquely in the first delusion-rooted consciousness.

reviewCards.front: What is Rootless consciousness (Ahetuka citta)?
reviewCards.back: Consciousness that arises without any of the six root conditions (greed, hatred, delusion, non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion) as concurrent associates — yet still arises from past kamma.

reviewCards.front: How are the 18 Rootless cittas classified?
reviewCards.back: Into two main types: 15 Rootless Resultant cittas (7 unwholesome resultants + 8 wholesome resultants) and 3 Rootless Functional cittas.

reviewCards.front: What are the seven Unwholesome Resultant cittas?
reviewCards.back: Eye, ear, nose, tongue consciousness (with equanimity); Body consciousness (with pain); Receiving consciousness (with equanimity); Investigating consciousness (with equanimity).

reviewCards.front: How does Body consciousness differ between unwholesome and wholesome resultants?
reviewCards.back: Unwholesome resultant: accompanied by physical PAIN (dukkha). Wholesome resultant: accompanied by physical PLEASURE (sukha). (The other four sense consciousnesses are accompanied by equanimity.)

reviewCards.front: What are the eight Wholesome Resultant Rootless cittas?
reviewCards.back: Eye, ear, nose, tongue consciousness (with equanimity); Body consciousness (with pleasure); Receiving consciousness (with equanimity); Investigating consciousness with equanimity; Investigating consciousness with joy.

reviewCards.front: What are the three Rootless Functional cittas?
reviewCards.back: Five-door adverting consciousness, Mind-door adverting consciousness (both with equanimity), and Smile-producing consciousness of Arahants (with joy).

reviewCards.front: What is the function of Five-door adverting consciousness (Pañcadvārāvajjana)?
reviewCards.back: When an object strikes a sense organ and disturbs the bhavaṅga stream, it adverts the mind to the sense door, then ceases, allowing sense consciousness to arise.

reviewCards.front: What is the function of Mind-door adverting consciousness (Manodvārāvajjana)?
reviewCards.back: Determining the object entering the mind and opening the path for javana cittas to perform active kamma.

reviewCards.front: Whose citta is the Smile-producing consciousness (Hasituppāda) and what feeling accompanies it?
reviewCards.back: It is a rootless functional citta accompanied by joy, unique to Arahants and Buddhas when smiling at mundane phenomena.

reviewCards.front: Why are they called "Unwholesome Resultant Rootless cittas"?
reviewCards.back: Because they are results produced by unwholesome kamma performed in the past — functioning as passive ripening in the present.

quizSeeds.question: Which roots are absent in Rootless consciousness?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: Greed, Hatred, Delusion, Non-greed, Non-hatred, Non-delusion
quizSeeds.explanation: Ahetuka cittas are devoid of all 6 conascent roots (hetus).

quizSeeds.question: How are the 18 Rootless cittas divided into resultants and functionals?
quizSeeds.explanation: 18 rootless cittas comprise 7 unwholesome resultants, 8 wholesome resultants, and 3 functionals.

quizSeeds.question: Among the 7 unwholesome resultant rootless cittas, which is accompanied by bodily PAIN?
quizSeeds.explanation: Unwholesome resultant body consciousness is accompanied by physical pain (dukkhasahagata).

quizSeeds.question: Among the 8 wholesome resultant rootless cittas, which is accompanied by bodily PLEASURE?
quizSeeds.explanation: Wholesome resultant body consciousness is accompanied by physical pleasure (sukhasahagata).

quizSeeds.question: What feelings can accompany the wholesome resultant Investigating consciousness?
quizSeeds.explanation: Santīraṇa kusala-vipāka occurs either accompanied by joy (somanassa) or accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā).

quizSeeds.question: To which class does Five-door adverting consciousness belong?
quizSeeds.explanation: Pañcadvārāvajjana is a rootless functional citta accompanied by equanimity (ahetukakiriya upekkhāsahagata).

quizSeeds.question: What feeling accompanies the Smile-producing consciousness (Hasituppāda)?
quizSeeds.explanation: Hasituppāda is accompanied by joy (somanassa) as the Arahant smiles at ordinary worldly situations.

quizSeeds.question: How many Rootless cittas are there in total?
quizSeeds.explanation: There are 18 ahetuka cittas: 7 akusala-vipāka + 8 kusala-vipāka + 3 kiriya.

quizSeeds.question: What does asynchronous cause-and-effect (nānākhaṇikakamma-vipāka) mean?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: The result arises at a different time from the past kamma that produced it
distractors: Cause and effect arise in the exact same moment
quizSeeds.explanation: Karmic fruit (vipāka) matures in subsequent moments or lifetimes through asynchronous kamma condition.

quizSeeds.question: What is the function of Mind-door adverting consciousness in a sense-door process?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: Determining (voṭṭhapana) the object before javana arises
distractors: Receiving the object from the sense organs
quizSeeds.explanation: In a five-door process, manodvārāvajjana performs the determining function (voṭṭhapana-kicca).

reviewCards.front: What does "Sobhana" mean?
reviewCards.back: Radiant, beautiful, pure, wholesome. Sobhana signifies purity, goodness, and ethical uprightness.

reviewCards.front: How many Beautiful mental factors (Sobhana cetasika) are there?
reviewCards.back: 25 mental factors, divided into 4 groups.

reviewCards.front: How many Universal Beautiful mental factors (Sobhanasādhāraṇa) are there?
reviewCards.back: 19 mental factors.

reviewCards.front: What are the first four mental factors in the 19 Beautiful Universals?
reviewCards.back: Faith (Saddhā), Mindfulness (Sati), Moral Shame (Hiri), and Moral Dread (Ottappa).

reviewCards.front: What are the 5th, 6th, and 7th mental factors in the 19 Beautiful Universals?
reviewCards.back: Non-greed (Alobha), Non-hatred (Adosa), and Equanimity / neutrality of mind (Tatramajjhattatā).

reviewCards.front: What are the six pairs of mental tranquility and proficiency?
reviewCards.back: Tranquility, lightness, pliancy, wieldiness, proficiency, and rectitude — each having a mental body (kāya) and consciousness (citta) component.

reviewCards.front: Moral Shame (Hiri) and Moral Dread (Ottappa) oppose which unwholesome factors?
reviewCards.back: Hiri opposes shamelessness (Ahirika); Ottappa opposes fearlessness of wrongdoing (Anottappa).

reviewCards.front: Which mental factors make up the Abstinences (Viratiyo)?
reviewCards.back: 3 mental factors: Right Speech (Sammāvācā), Right Action (Sammākammanta), and Right Livelihood (Sammā-ājīva).

reviewCards.front: What are Kāyapassaddhi and Cittapassaddhi?
reviewCards.back: Tranquility of mental body (associated cetasikas) and tranquility of consciousness — the first pair of the six twin pairs.

reviewCards.front: What are the final two mental factors of the 19 Beautiful Universals?
reviewCards.back: Rectitude of mental body (Kāyujjukatā) and rectitude of consciousness (Cittujjukatā).

reviewCards.front: What are the four sub-groups of the 25 Beautiful mental factors?
reviewCards.back: 19 Beautiful Universals + 3 Abstinences + 2 Illimitables + 1 Wisdom Faculty = 25.

reviewCards.front: Which mental factors make up the Illimitables (Appamaññā)?
reviewCards.back: 2 mental factors: Compassion (Karuṇā) and Sympathetic Joy (Muditā).

reviewCards.front: What four kinds of verbal misconduct does Right Speech (Sammāvācā) abstain from?
reviewCards.back: False speech (musāvāda), slanderous speech (pisuṇāvācā), harsh speech (pharusavācā), and idle chatter (samphappalāpa).

reviewCards.front: What three bodily unwholesome actions does Right Action (Sammākammanta) eradicate?
reviewCards.back: Killing living beings, stealing, and sexual misconduct.

reviewCards.front: What is Right Livelihood (Sammā-ājīva)?
reviewCards.back: Righteous way of living and earning — refraining from earning one's livelihood through bodily or verbal misconduct.

reviewCards.front: What is Compassion (Karuṇā)?
reviewCards.back: The trembling of a noble heart at the suffering of other beings; wishing to remove their suffering and torment.

reviewCards.front: What is Sympathetic Joy (Muditā)?
reviewCards.back: Gladness and rejoicing in the happiness and prosperity of others, free from envy.

reviewCards.front: What is the characteristic of the Faculty of Wisdom (Paññindriya)?
reviewCards.back: Penetrating comprehension and insight — seeing ultimate realities as they truly are, dissipating the darkness of ignorance.

reviewCards.front: In the six pairs, what do "Body" (Kāya) and "Consciousness" (Citta) denote?
reviewCards.back: Kāya denotes the mental body: the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations (the associated cetasikas); Citta denotes the consciousness aggregate (citta).

reviewCards.front: What are the three wholesome roots?
reviewCards.back: Non-greed (Alobha), Non-hatred (Adosa), and Non-delusion (Amoha / Paññā) — co-arising in beautiful consciousness as the roots of good.

quizSeeds.question: How many Beautiful Universal mental factors (Sobhanasādhāraṇa) are there?
quizSeeds.explanation: There are 19 Beautiful Universals present in every beautiful citta.

quizSeeds.question: How many mental factors comprise the entire Beautiful (Sobhana) group?
quizSeeds.explanation: The 25 Sobhana cetasikas are: 19 universals, 3 abstinences, 2 illimitables, and 1 wisdom faculty.

quizSeeds.question: What does the term "Sobhana" signify?
quizSeeds.explanation: Sobhana means beautiful, wholesome, lovely, and luminous.

quizSeeds.question: Which mental factor heads the 19 Beautiful Universals?
quizSeeds.explanation: Saddhā (faith/confidence) is the foremost of the 19 Beautiful Universals.

quizSeeds.question: What is Tatramajjhattatā?
quizSeeds.explanation: Tatramajjhattatā has the characteristic of conveying citta and cetasikas evenly and neutrally.

quizSeeds.question: How many mental factors make up the Abstinences (Viratiyo)?
quizSeeds.explanation: The three abstinences are Right Speech, Right Action, and Right Livelihood.

quizSeeds.question: Which factor does NOT belong to the Abstinences (Viratiyo)?
quizSeeds.explanation: Right Mindfulness is Sati, which is a Beautiful Universal, not an Abstinence.

quizSeeds.question: What pair are Kāyalahutā and Cittalahutā?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: Lightness of mental body and lightness of consciousness
quizSeeds.explanation: Lahutā refers to lightness or buoyancy, opposing heaviness and sluggishness.

quizSeeds.question: How many twin pairs of mental body and consciousness are there in the 19 Beautiful Universals?
quizSeeds.explanation: There are 6 pairs (12 cetasikas): passaddhi, lahutā, mudutā, kammaññatā, pāguññatā, and ujjukatā.

quizSeeds.question: Moral Shame (Hiri) is the direct opposite of which factor?
quizSeeds.explanation: Hiri (moral shame) directly opposes Ahirika (moral shamelessness).

quizSeeds.question: How many mental factors make up the Illimitables (Appamaññā)?
quizSeeds.explanation: Mettā is adosa and Upekkhā is tatramajjhattatā; thus the Appamaññā group contains 2 distinct cetasikas: Karuṇā and Muditā.

quizSeeds.question: How many mental factors comprise the Faculty of Wisdom (Paññindriya)?
quizSeeds.explanation: The Faculty of Wisdom is a single mental factor: Paññindriya (non-delusion, amoha).

quizSeeds.question: To which group do the Abstinences (Viratiyo) belong?
quizSeeds.explanation: The Abstinences form a distinct sub-group within the 25 Beautiful mental factors.

quizSeeds.question: What four types of verbal misconduct does Right Speech abstain from?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: False speech, slander, harsh speech, and idle chatter
distractors: False speech, slander, harsh speech, praising others
False speech, sharing Dhamma, harsh speech, silence
quizSeeds.explanation: Right Speech abstains from the fourfold verbal misconduct: musāvāda, pisuṇāvācā, pharusavācā, and samphappalāpa.

quizSeeds.question: What three bodily unwholesome actions does Right Action abstain from?
quizSeeds.explanation: Right Action abstains from bodily harm: pāṇātipātā, adinnādānā, and kāmesumicchācārā.

quizSeeds.question: Which mental factor is Sammā-ājīva?
quizSeeds.explanation: Sammā-ājīva is the mental factor of Right Livelihood.

quizSeeds.question: How does Sympathetic Joy (Muditā) differ from Compassion (Karuṇā)?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: Compassion targets suffering beings; Sympathetic Joy rejoices in the success of others
distractors: Compassion rejoices in joy; Sympathetic Joy grieves over suffering
Both rejoice in prosperous beings exclusively
quizSeeds.explanation: Karuṇā takes suffering beings as object, while Muditā takes prosperous, happy beings as object.

quizSeeds.question: What is the characteristic of the Faculty of Wisdom (Paññindriya)?
quizSeeds.explanation: Paññindriya illuminates things as they truly are, destroying the dark veil of moha.

quizSeeds.question: Which unwholesome factors are directly opposed by Lightness of body and mind (Kāyalahutā / Cittalahutā)?
quizSeeds.explanation: Lightness banishes the heaviness, rigidity, and sluggishness of thīna and middha.

quizSeeds.question: What are the three kinds of Wisdom according to development?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: Wisdom born of learning, wisdom born of reflection, wisdom born of meditation
quizSeeds.explanation: The three types of wisdom are sutamayā paññā, cintāmayā paññā, and bhāvanāmayā paññā.

reviewCards.front: How many Sense-sphere Beautiful cittas are there and how are they grouped?
reviewCards.back: 24 cittas, divided into 3 groups: 8 Great Wholesome (Mahākusala), 8 Great Resultant (Mahāvipāka), and 8 Great Functional (Mahākiriya).

reviewCards.front: Why are they called "Great Wholesome" (Mahākusala)?
reviewCards.back: Because they perform vast wholesome actions — the Ten Bases of Meritorious Action (puññakiriyavatthu).

reviewCards.front: What is Great Resultant consciousness (Mahāvipāka)?
reviewCards.back: The karmic fruition resulting from past Great Wholesome actions.

reviewCards.front: What cittas do Arahants experience instead of Great Wholesome?
reviewCards.back: Great Functional cittas (Mahākiriya) — because they no longer generate new karmic causes.

reviewCards.front: By what three pairs of opposites are the 8 Great Wholesome cittas classified?
reviewCards.back: Accompanied by joy / equanimity; Associated with / dissociated from knowledge; Unprompted / prompted.

reviewCards.front: What is the key distinction between the 8 Greed cittas and 8 Great Wholesome cittas?
reviewCards.back: Greed cittas are classified by Wrong View (associated/dissociated); Great Wholesome cittas are classified by Knowledge/Wisdom (associated/dissociated).

reviewCards.front: What does "Ñāṇasampayutta" mean?
reviewCards.back: Associated with knowledge — accompanied by wisdom or understanding of reality.

reviewCards.front: What do "Sobhana" and "Kāmāvacara" mean?
reviewCards.back: Sobhana: beautiful, pure, wholesome. Kāmāvacara: frequently arising within the sense realm.

reviewCards.front: In which beings can Great Wholesome cittas arise?
reviewCards.back: Hungry ghosts, animals, hell beings (temporarily), humans, devas, and noble disciples in training (sekkha) — except Arahants.

reviewCards.front: What is the full Pāḷi name of the first Great Wholesome citta?
reviewCards.back: Somanassa-sahagataṁ ñāṇasampayuttaṁ asaṅkhārikaṁ ekaṁ — one citta accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, unprompted.

quizSeeds.question: How many Sense-sphere Beautiful cittas are there?
quizSeeds.explanation: The 24 sense-sphere beautiful cittas comprise 8 Mahākusala, 8 Mahāvipāka, and 8 Mahākiriya.

quizSeeds.question: For which class of individuals are the Great Functional (Mahākiriya) cittas?
quizSeeds.explanation: Mahākiriya cittas arise only in Arahants, who perform bodily, verbal, and mental actions without generating kamma.

quizSeeds.question: By which factor are the 8 Great Wholesome cittas differentiated (unlike Greed cittas)?
distractors: Associated with / dissociated from wrong view (diṭṭhi)
quizSeeds.explanation: Greed cittas differ by diṭṭhi, while Great Wholesome cittas differ by ñāṇa (knowledge/wisdom).

quizSeeds.question: What is Great Resultant consciousness (Mahāvipāka)?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: The karmic fruition of Great Wholesome actions
quizSeeds.explanation: Mahāvipāka is the direct result of sense-sphere wholesome kamma.

quizSeeds.question: What does the designation "Great" (Mahā) imply in Great Wholesome?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: Capably performing vast merit through the Ten Bases of Meritorious Action
distractors: Containing the highest number of mental factors
Ripening exclusively in the form sphere
quizSeeds.explanation: Mahā indicates the extensive scope of wholesome deeds (generosity, morality, meditation, etc.) performed by these cittas.

quizSeeds.question: What are the characteristics of the first Great Wholesome citta?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: Accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, unprompted
distractors: Accompanied by equanimity, dissociated from knowledge, prompted
Accompanied by joy, associated with wrong view, unprompted
Accompanied by displeasure, associated with aversion, unprompted
quizSeeds.explanation: Citta 1 of Mahākusala is somanassa-sahagata, ñāṇasampayutta, asaṅkhārika.

quizSeeds.question: How many cittas are in each sub-group of Sense-sphere Beautiful consciousness?
quizSeeds.explanation: Each of the 3 sub-groups (wholesome, resultant, functional) contains exactly 8 cittas.

quizSeeds.question: What does "Sobhana" mean?
quizSeeds.explanation: Sobhana means beautiful, wholesome, lovely, and luminous.

quizSeeds.question: In which individuals do Great Wholesome cittas NOT arise?
quizSeeds.explanation: Arahants experience Great Functional (Mahākiriya) cittas instead of Great Wholesome (Mahākusala) cittas.

quizSeeds.question: What does "Ñāṇavippayutta" mean?
quizSeeds.explanation: Ñāṇavippayutta denotes consciousness that is wholesome but unaccompanied by insight or wisdom.

reviewCards.front: What is Sublime consciousness (Mahaggata citta)?
reviewCards.back: MAHA (great) + GATA (reached) -> consciousness that has reached greatness and tranquility; 27 cittas (15 Form-sphere + 12 Formless-sphere).

reviewCards.front: What is Form-sphere consciousness (Rūpāvacara citta)?
reviewCards.back: Consciousness that frequently recurs and belongs to the Form realm.

reviewCards.front: How are the 15 Form-sphere cittas divided?
reviewCards.back: 3 groups: Wholesome, Resultant, Functional — each comprising 5 Jhāna levels.

reviewCards.front: Which jhāna factors accompany the First Jhāna?
reviewCards.back: Applied Thought (Vitakka), Sustained Thought (Vicāra), Joy (Pīti), Bliss (Sukha), and One-pointedness (Ekaggatā).

reviewCards.front: How does the Second Jhāna differ from the First Jhāna?
reviewCards.back: Eliminates Applied Thought (Vitakka) — remaining: Sustained Thought, Joy, Bliss, One-pointedness.

reviewCards.front: Which jhāna factors remain in the Third Jhāna?
reviewCards.back: Joy (Pīti), Bliss (Sukha), and One-pointedness (Ekaggatā) — having eliminated both Vitakka and Vicāra.

reviewCards.front: What factors accompany the Fourth and Fifth Jhānas?
reviewCards.back: Fourth Jhāna: Bliss + One-pointedness (eliminating Joy). Fifth Jhāna: Equanimity (Upekkhā) + One-pointedness (changing Bliss to Equanimity).

reviewCards.front: From where does Form-sphere Resultant consciousness arise?
reviewCards.back: Ripening from past Form-sphere wholesome jhāna attainment.

reviewCards.front: How does Form-sphere Functional consciousness differ from Wholesome?
reviewCards.back: Functional generates no kamma and produces no vipāka — it is the jhāna consciousness of Arahants.

reviewCards.front: What are five benefits of developing Samatha meditation?
reviewCards.back: Present pleasant dwelling; foundation for vipassanā; direct knowledge/supernormal powers (5 abhiññās); rebirth in Brahmā realms; attainment of Nirodhasamāpatti.

quizSeeds.question: How many Sublime (Mahaggata) cittas are there?
quizSeeds.explanation: Mahaggata cittas comprise 15 Form-sphere + 12 Formless-sphere cittas = 27.

quizSeeds.question: What does "Rūpāvacaracitta" mean?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: Consciousness that frequents and belongs to the Form realm
distractors: Consciousness found only in sense realm
quizSeeds.explanation: Rūpāvacara denotes consciousness that moves in or pertains to the plane of subtle form.

quizSeeds.question: How are the 15 Form-sphere cittas structured?
quizSeeds.explanation: The 15 Form-sphere cittas consist of 5 kusala, 5 vipāka, and 5 kiriya cittas.

quizSeeds.question: Which jhāna factors accompany the First Jhāna (Paṭhamajjhāna)?
quizSeeds.explanation: The fivefold First Jhāna comprises vitakka, vicāra, pīti, sukha, and ekaggatā.

quizSeeds.question: Which jhāna factor is eliminated in the Second Jhāna (Dutiyajjhāna)?
quizSeeds.explanation: In the Abhidhamma 5-fold scheme, the second jhāna drops Vitakka while retaining Vicāra.

quizSeeds.question: What feeling accompanies the Fifth Jhāna wholesome citta?
quizSeeds.explanation: In the Fifth Jhāna, bliss (sukha) is replaced by neutral feeling (upekkhā).

quizSeeds.question: What is Form-sphere Resultant consciousness (Rūpāvacara Vipāka)?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: The fruition of past Form-sphere wholesome jhāna kamma
quizSeeds.explanation: Rūpāvacara vipāka arises as rebirth-linking, bhavaṅga, and death cittas in the Brahmā form realms.

quizSeeds.question: What is the fundamental difference among the five Form Jhānas?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: Progressive shedding of coarser jhāna factors (Vitakka, Vicāra, Pīti, and replacing Sukha with Upekkhā)
distractors: Different material bases in Brahmā worlds
quizSeeds.explanation: The jhāna levels are distinguished by the successive elimination of coarse jhāna factors.

quizSeeds.question: Upon mastering the Fifth Form Jhāna, how many mundane supernormal knowledges (abhiññā) can be developed?
quizSeeds.explanation: Mastery of the 5th jhāna provides the basis for the 5 mundane abhiññās (divine eye, divine ear, psychic powers, mind-reading, recollection of past lives).

quizSeeds.question: What qualification is needed to attain the Cessation of Perception and Feeling (Nirodhasamāpatti)?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: Non-returners or Arahants who have mastered all 8 meditative attainments
distractors: Anyone who attains the First Jhāna
quizSeeds.explanation: Nirodhasamāpatti is attainable only by Anāgāmīs and Arahants endowed with the 8 samāpattis.

reviewCards.front: In what three senses is consciousness termed "Formless" (Arūpāvacara)?
reviewCards.back: 1) Takes formless meditation subjects as object; 2) Results in rebirth in the formless realms; 3) Frequents the formless realm.

reviewCards.front: What are the four Formless Meditative Attainments?
reviewCards.back: Base of Boundless Space, Base of Boundless Consciousness, Base of Nothingness, Base of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.

reviewCards.front: What does "Ākāsānañcāyatana" mean?
reviewCards.back: Ākāsa (space) + ananta (endless) + āyatana (base) -> Base of Boundless Space.

reviewCards.front: How does one attain the Base of Boundless Space?
reviewCards.back: Contemplating the defects of matter; attaining 5th form jhāna with a kasiṇa; discarding kasiṇa image and focusing on infinite space.

reviewCards.front: What is the object of the Base of Boundless Consciousness?
reviewCards.back: It takes the consciousness of the Base of Boundless Space as its object, noting "infinite consciousness".

reviewCards.front: What is the object of the Base of Nothingness?
reviewCards.back: It takes the non-existence/absence of the boundless space consciousness as object, noting "there is nothing".

reviewCards.front: What is special about the Base of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception?
reviewCards.back: Taking the Base of Nothingness as object, its perception is so refined that it can neither be said to exist nor not to exist.

reviewCards.front: Which jhāna factors are present in Formless Jhānas?
reviewCards.back: Only two factors: Equanimity (Upekkhā) and One-pointedness (Ekaggatā) — identical in factor structure to the 5th form jhāna, differing by object subtlety.

reviewCards.front: How are the 12 Formless-sphere cittas grouped?
reviewCards.back: 3 groups: 4 Wholesome, 4 Resultant, 4 Functional — corresponding to the 4 formless realms.

reviewCards.front: Whose consciousness is Formless Functional consciousness?
reviewCards.back: Arahants who attain formless jhānas — producing no karmic results.

quizSeeds.question: How many Formless-sphere cittas are there?
quizSeeds.explanation: There are 12 Arūpāvacara cittas: 4 wholesome, 4 resultant, and 4 functional.

quizSeeds.question: What are the four Formless bases?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: Boundless Space, Boundless Consciousness, Nothingness, Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception
distractors: Boundless Space, Boundless Joy, Nothingness, Neither-Perception
quizSeeds.explanation: The 4 formless jhānas are Ākāsānañcāyatana, Viññāṇañcāyatana, Ākiñcaññāyatana, and Nevasaññānāsaññāyatana.

quizSeeds.question: Which base is "Ākāsānañcāyatana"?
quizSeeds.explanation: Ākāsānañcāyatana is the Base of Boundless Space.

quizSeeds.question: To cultivate formless meditation, what must the meditator first perceive?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: The perils and grossness of physical matter and desire to detach from matter
quizSeeds.explanation: The practitioner sees the defects of the physical body and matter, aspiring to transcend form.

quizSeeds.question: What serves as the object for the Base of Boundless Consciousness?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: The consciousness of the Base of Boundless Space
distractors: The subtle matter of Brahmā realms
quizSeeds.explanation: Viññāṇañcāyatana takes the preceding ākāsānañcāyatana citta as its meditation object.

quizSeeds.question: How many jhāna factors are present in Formless Jhānas?
quizSeeds.explanation: All 4 formless jhānas have exactly 2 jhāna factors: upekkhā and ekaggatā.

quizSeeds.question: Which base is "Nevasaññā-nāsaññāyatana"?
quizSeeds.explanation: Nevasaññā-nāsaññāyatana is the fourth and highest formless attainment.

quizSeeds.question: What type of object does Formless consciousness cognize?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: Immaterial/formless meditation object — not physical matter
distractors: Five sense objects (sights, sounds, smells, tastes, touches)
quizSeeds.explanation: Formless consciousness takes non-material objects (space, past consciousness, absence, refined mental state).

quizSeeds.question: What is the fruition of wholesome formless jhāna kamma?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: Rebirth in the corresponding Formless Brahmā realm
quizSeeds.explanation: Arūpāvacara kusala leads directly to rebirth in one of the 4 Arūpaloka planes.

quizSeeds.question: Whose consciousness is the Formless Functional citta?
quizSeeds.correctAnswer: An Arahant who attains formless meditative absorptions
quizSeeds.explanation: Formless functional cittas (arūpa-kiriya) belong exclusively to Arahants.
